source: original; stimulus table compiled from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics annual averages

stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics, annual averages for 1970 and 1980. Account drawn from the grounding books (Barron's Ch. 10, Topic 8.14; 5 Steps Ch. 28; Princeton Ch. 12).
stimulus.text:
Jobs by sector (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics, annual averages):

| Year | Total nonfarm jobs | Manufacturing jobs | Manufacturing share of all jobs | Service-providing share of all jobs |
| 1970 | 70.9 million | 17.8 million | 25% | 69% |
| 1980 | 90.7 million | 18.7 million | 21% | 73% |

stem: The table best supports which claim about the service economy in the 1970s?

options.text: Service jobs grew faster than factory jobs, so services took a larger share.
Factory jobs disappeared entirely by 1980 as plants closed in every part of the country.
options.misconception: The table shows 18.7 million manufacturing jobs in 1980, so factory jobs did not disappear.

options.text: Total jobs fell through the 1970s as the whole economy shrank year after year.
options.misconception: The table shows total jobs rising from 70.9 million to 90.7 million.

options.text: Services shrank through the 1970s while factories grew and hired more workers.
options.misconception: The table shows the service share rising from 69 percent to 73 percent.

rationales.A: Total jobs grew by about 20 million while factory jobs grew by under 1 million, so the growth went to services, whose share rose to 73 percent.
rationales.B: The table shows 18.7 million manufacturing jobs in 1980, so factory jobs did not disappear.
rationales.C: The table shows total jobs rising from 70.9 million to 90.7 million, not falling.
rationales.D: The table shows the service share rising from 69 percent to 73 percent, so services did not shrink.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the growth: total jobs rose by about 20 million, but factory jobs rose by under 1 million.
2. That extra growth had to go somewhere, and the service share rose from 69 percent to 73 percent.
3. So services grew faster than factories and took a larger share of all jobs.
Remember: When one part grows slowly and the whole grows fast, the fast-growing parts gain share.
